warmup.q: Two agents edit the note "pay 40" at the same moment. Positions count from 0, so the 4 is at position 4. Agent a types "$" at position 4, before the 4. Agent b types "!" at position 6, the end. Each laptop applies its own edit, then the other's edit exactly as it was sent. What does agent a's laptop show?
options: "pay $40!": both edits are inserts, so the order doesn't matter
"pay $4!0": position 6 meant "after the 0" in b's text, but a's text has an extra character before it
"pay 40!": the later edit replaces the earlier one
It depends on which laptop's clock is ahead
warmup.why: Inserts at positions give different results in different orders. a's text is pay $40, seven characters, so inserting ! at position 6 puts it between the 4 and the 0. b's laptop applies a's $ at position 4 to pay 40! and gets pay $40!, so the two laptops now disagree. The first option is the tempting one, and it's what b's laptop shows, by luck. No clock is involved. The fix is to adjust the position (operational transformation, the third section) or to stop sending positions at all (a CRDT, the last section).

sections.h: A copy on the device: reads and writes that never wait for the network
sections.html:
Let's time the agent's clicks. The agent works in a dispute console, the app support staff use to look into a customer's complaint about a payment. Each complaint is a case called a dispute, such as DSP-311. Every click in the console waits for a round trip to the server: 150 ms from a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi to a server on another continent. A screen redraws every 16 ms at 60 Hz (60 times a second), so the agent watches nine frames of spinner per click. On a train with no signal, clicks fail outright.

A cache, a saved copy of the server's recent answers, fixes part of this. Reads come back at once, though possibly out of date, but nothing can be written offline. The next step is the one Many leaders (lesson 5) took for regions: put a copy, and a leader, where the writes happen. A leader is a place that accepts writes and puts them in order. The browser or the phone keeps its own copy of the agent's data. On a phone that's often SQLite, a small database that lives in one file; in a web browser, it's IndexedDB, a database the browser has built in. Every read and write goes to that copy and finishes within one frame.

A sync engine, a library on the device plus a service on the server, sends local changes up and other people's changes down whenever there's a network. Going offline becomes copying that runs two hours late, with no special mode in the app.

This is multi-leader replication, keeping copies that each take writes, with one leader per device. So lesson 5's problem comes along, the write conflict: two agents can change the same dispute while one of them is offline, and neither sees the other's change. There are new costs too. The data has to fit on the device, which works for one agent's open cases and not for a bank's full history of card payments. And the server can no longer check each write as it happens, because some writes reach it hours later.

In 2019, Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg and Mark McGranaghan of the research lab Ink & Switch named this style in an essay, Local-first software, with seven ideals. In short: no spinners, and your work isn't trapped on one device. The network is optional, and working with colleagues just works. Your data outlives the software (they called this the long now), security and privacy come by default, and you keep ownership and control.

The last ones ask for more than working offline. A local-first app keeps working if the company behind it shuts down its servers. That takes an open sync protocol, rules for syncing that anyone can build on, and not only a local copy. Their prototypes used Automerge, a library of CRDTs: data types whose copies merge to the same result in any order (lesson 8 builds some). Merging was almost always painless, and conflicts were rare in practice. The trouble was size, since keeping every edit forever soon caused speed and memory problems.

The device holds a copy and leads its own writes. So the design question is lesson 5's: who decides the order of concurrent writes, the ones made at the same time with neither knowing of the other? The next section answers "the server". The last two answer "nobody", for text.

t=   800  set reason: not received     on screen after 150 ms
t= 2,500  attach courier receipt       spinner for 5 s, then a network error: retype it later

t= 9,000  set status: under review     spinner for 5 s, then a network error: retype it later

Design 1 loses three clicks and 15 seconds of spinners. Design 2 shows every click in one frame, and turns the outage into 10 seconds of delay in the copying. (The last click hands the case to the team that handles chargebacks, money a bank takes back from a shop after a dispute.) Look at what design 2 assumes, though: three changes sat on the laptop, unseen by anyone, for up to 9.5 seconds. If agent B closed DSP-311 during that time, the server has to decide what happens to them, which is the next section.

sections.h: Let the server order the writes: changes shown at once, then a rebase
sections.html:
Most business apps have a server anyway, and the simplest answer to lesson 5's question is to let it decide. The scheme is called server reconciliation. The sync engine of Linear, an app teams use to track their work, uses a version of it, and so do Replicache, its successor Zero, and PowerSync.

The client, the app on the laptop, runs every change twice. A change is written as a mutation, a named action such as addNote(dispute, text). First the mutation runs on the local copy, at once, and goes into a queue. A change shown before the server has accepted it is called optimistic: the app hopes the server will agree. Then the server runs the same mutation, in its own order, on the real database, with whatever checks it needs.

The server is a single leader, like the one in One leader, many followers (lesson 1). It applies mutations one at a time, gives each change it accepts the next number, and sends the resulting rows to every client, including the one that sent the mutation. When that answer arrives, the client throws away its own guesses and takes the server's state, its version of the data. Then it runs again, on top of it, the mutations the server hasn't answered yet. That re-run is a rebase, a word borrowed from git, the tool programmers use to keep versions of their code. A mutation the server rejected leaves the queue, and the screen goes back.

The stepper follows two agents on one dispute. Agent B closes it. Agent A, who hasn't heard, adds a note and sets a reason. B's close reaches the server first. The server rejects A's note, because notes can't be added to a closed dispute, and accepts the reason. A's screen showed the note for about 100 ms; then the rebase removed it, and the app told A why. Nothing had to be merged, because the rule ran once, on the server, at a definite point in the order.

The products differ in the details. A detailed study of Linear's web app, endorsed by Linear's chief technology officer, describes edits applied in the browser's memory at once, queued in IndexedDB and run by the server. The server gives every change an increasing sync id and pushes the changes to all clients over a WebSocket, a connection that stays open both ways. A rejected change is rolled back on the client.

In Zero (1.0 in 2026, from Rocicorp, which also made Replicache), mutators, its name for mutations, run on the client first. Then the server runs its own version in a transaction, a group of changes saved together or not at all, against Postgres (short for PostgreSQL, a free database program). There it can check who may do what. Changes reach Zero's cache through Postgres logical replication, the row log of Replication logs (lesson 2). The client drops a mutation's local effects once the server's rows for it arrive.

PowerSync keeps an SQLite database on the device and puts local writes in an upload queue, first in, first out. It then calls an uploadData() function you write, which sends them to your own server. ElectricSQL (1.0 in March 2025) does only the read half. It follows Postgres logical replication and serves chosen subsets of rows, which it calls shapes, to clients, while writes go through your own server.

The common cost: a change isn't final until the server has seen it. An agent who works offline for two hours works on guesses, and some may come back rejected.

That suits a status or a reason, where one value should win. Next, we'll meet data where nobody's change should be thrown away: two people typing in the same note.

try.title: Watch a mutation get rejected and the queue rebase
steps: Read serverRun in RebaseDemo.kt: the server's version of each mutation has one rule the client's lacks.
Predict what agent A sees at t=95 and at t=110. Then run it.
Move B's close after A's mutations (put the serve(60, n1) line below the two serve(7x, ...) lines) and predict again: which mutation is rejected now?
try.expect:
t=10   agent A clicks addNote(customer called)   sees status=OPEN reason=- notes=[customer called]   (pending 1)
t=12   agent B clicks close()                    sees status=CLOSED reason=- notes=[]   (pending 1)
t=20   agent A clicks setReason(not received)    sees status=OPEN reason=not received notes=[customer called]   (pending 2)
t=60   server applies b1 close as sync id 42
t=75   server rejects a1 addNote: the dispute is CLOSED
t=76   server applies a2 setReason as sync id 43
t=95   agent A clicks setReason(damaged)         sees status=OPEN reason=damaged notes=[customer called]   (pending 3)
       server log: [42:b1, 43:a2]   state: status=CLOSED reason=not received notes=[]
t=110  agent A a1 was rejected: rolled back, the agent is told
t=110  agent A rebases on sync id 43, re-runs 1 pending, sees status=CLOSED reason=damaged notes=[]
t=115  agent B rebases on sync id 43, re-runs 0 pending, sees status=CLOSED reason=not received notes=[]
t=130  server applies a3 setReason as sync id 44
t=170  agent A rebases on sync id 44, re-runs 0 pending, sees status=CLOSED reason=damaged notes=[]

Until t=110, A's screen is a guess built on a dispute that was already closed. The rebase replaces it with the server's state plus the one mutation still on its way. With B's close moved last, nothing is rejected: the note and both reasons land first, and the close applies after them as sync id 44. Same mutations, different order, different outcome, and every client agrees on it, because the server chose the order.

sections.h: Two people typing in one note: operational transformation
sections.html:
Server reconciliation chooses between whole mutations. Text needs something finer. Two agents typing into the same note at the same moment both expect their characters to survive, and keeping one version of the note throws away the other person's typing.

Start with the simplest way to describe an edit: insert a character at a position, counting from 0. The note says pay 40. Agent a types $ before the 4, which is insert '$' at 4, and sees pay $40. At the same moment agent b types ! at the end, insert '!' at 6, and sees pay 40!. Each sends its edit to the other. b applies a's edit and gets pay $40!. a applies b's edit as sent and gets pay $4!0. Position 6 meant "after the 0" in b's text, and a's text has grown by one character in front of that spot.

Operational transformation (OT) fixes the position before applying it. Say an edit arrives that was made at the same time as one you've already applied. Transform it against yours: if yours landed before its position, shift it right by one. Site a, agent a's copy of the note, shifts b's ! from 6 to 7 and gets pay $40!. When both insert at the same position, every site needs the same tie rule, such as "the smaller site name goes first", or the sites drift apart. Google Docs is built on OT.

Two sites with one edit each is the easy case. With many edits on their way, each one has to be transformed against every edit it was concurrent with, in an order every site agrees on. Most OT systems get that order from a central server. It receives each edit along with the last server version the sender had seen. It transforms the edit against everything applied since, and sends the result to everyone. That's the grid the lab's transformBoth works out. Without a server, the transform rules need extra properties that are much harder to get right, which is a large part of why OT has stayed tied to a server.

OT keeps no extra data per character: the note is a plain string, and an edit is a position and a character. Its weak spot is a long split. Merging two branches, copies of a document that were edited apart for days, means transforming every edit on one side against every edit on the other. In the Eg-walker paper (Joseph Gentle and Martin Kleppmann, at EuroSys 2025, a computer systems conference), merging one such pair of branches with OT took an hour.

The trouble comes from positions that shift under each other. Next, we'll stop sending positions at all.

try.title: Replay a position, then transform it
steps: Read transform in OtDemo.kt. It's one line: shift the incoming insert if the local one landed before it.
Predict what each site shows for the edit replayed as sent and for the transformed one, and for two inserts at the same position. Then run it.
try.expect:
site a: "pay 40" -> insert '$' at 4 -> "pay $40"
    receives insert '!' at 6
    replayed as sent:  "pay $4!0"
    transformed to insert '!' at 7: "pay $40!"
site b: "pay 40" -> insert '!' at 6 -> "pay 40!"
    receives insert '$' at 4
    replayed as sent:  "pay $40!"
    transformed to insert '$' at 4: "pay $40!"

same index on both sites: the smaller site name goes first, everywhere
site a: "pay xy40"   site b: "pay xy40"

Site b gets the right answer even without transforming, by luck: a's edit was before b's, so b's insert didn't move it. Site a needs the shift. With both inserts at position 4, a keeps its x and b moves its y one place right, so both read pay xy40. Change the tie rule on one site only, and they drift apart.

aside.title: Why not let only one person type at a time?
aside.html: That's a lock: whoever holds it may type, and everyone else waits. Taking the lock needs a round trip to whoever hands it out, so it brings back the spinner from the opening. An agent on a train can't take it at all. And a lock that someone forgot to give back blocks everyone until it times out. People also expect to type in the same note together, the way they do in Google Docs, so editors merge the edits instead.

sections.h: A text CRDT names every character, and keeps the names
sections.html:
A CRDT for text never has to transform anything, because it never sends positions. CRDT stands for conflict-free replicated data type: a data type whose copies can take edits apart and still merge to the same result. Every character gets a permanent id when it's typed, and an insert says which character it goes after.

Picture a printed page with a small serial number under every letter. Instead of "put this at position 5", each person writes "put this after letter 4a". Anyone can apply the notes in any order and get the same page. The picture breaks on deletes. On paper you'd rub a letter out, but here someone's note may still say "after this one".

In the lab's version, RGA (replicated growable array), an id is a counter plus a site name. When site a types pay 40, its characters get the ids 1a to 6a. The counter works like a Lamport clock, named after the computer scientist who described it. Each site's next id is one more than the highest counter it has seen from anyone. So a character typed after another always has a bigger counter. Agent a's $ travels as "insert $ named 7a after 4a" (the space), and b's ! as "insert ! named 7b after 6a" (the 0). Neither edit mentions a position, so neither needs transforming, and both sites end with pay $40!, as the figure shows. When two inserts name the same character, the bigger id goes first, on every site. A delete only marks its character as gone. That mark, a tombstone, has to stay, because an insert made at the same time somewhere may still name that character.

So a CRDT works in any delivery order, with no server in the middle, as long as an edit waits until the character it names has arrived. Automerge and Yjs are CRDT libraries built on ideas like this one. Riak, Redis Enterprise and Azure Cosmos DB, three databases, use CRDTs for other kinds of data.

The price is extra data, and it only grows. In this section's Try it, 10,000 random edits leave 2,136 visible characters and 6,068 kept nodes, one per character ever typed. That's 17 bytes of ids and flags per visible character, against zero for a plain string. Real libraries carry more. In Automerge 2, pasting Moby Dick, a long novel, into a document took 700 MB of memory. Automerge 3 (2025) keeps its compressed format in memory as well as on disk, and the same paste takes 1.3 MB.

Eg-walker goes further. It stores the plain edit history, like OT, and builds CRDT-style data only while merging, and only for the stretch where branches were edited at the same time. Its paper reports one to two orders of magnitude (10 to 100 times) less memory than the best CRDTs, and documents that load orders of magnitude faster. The hour-long OT merge took it 24 ms.

A CRDT promises that the copies agree, not that the result is what anyone meant. Two agents who fix the same typo at once can end up with the fix typed twice, and a rule such as "at most five attachments" can still be broken by two concurrent adds. Concurrent writes (lesson 8) builds CRDT counters and sets, and shows where they stop.

try.title: Merge by name, then count the cost
steps: Run RgaDemo.kt. It replays the two edits from the third section with ids instead of positions, then makes 10,000 random edits on one site.
Before it prints, predict the order of the ids after the merge. Then guess roughly how many bytes of extra data per visible character 10,000 edits leave behind when 40% of them are deletes.
try.expect:
both sites: p:1a a:2a y:3a  :4a 4:5a 0:6a
a sends insert '$' named 7a after 4a
b sends insert '!' named 7b after 6a
site a: "pay $40!"   site b: "pay $40!"
ids now: p:1a a:2a y:3a  :4a $:7a 4:5a 0:6a !:7b

10,000 random edits: 6068 inserts, 3932 deletes
visible characters: 2136   nodes kept: 6068   tombstones: 3932
metadata: 36408 bytes, 17.0 bytes per visible character (plain text: 0)

The ids are no longer in counter order (7a sits between 4a and 5a), and that's fine: a character's place comes from the one it was inserted after, and the counter only breaks ties. Every insert ever made is still there, 3,932 of them as tombstones, so the site keeps almost three nodes for each character you can see. The demo counts only 6 bytes per node (a 4-byte counter, a 1-byte site name, a 1-byte flag). Real libraries keep more about each insert, and an object in memory for each character costs far more than 6 bytes, which is how Automerge 2 reached 700 MB.

opening:
Picture a support agent at the payments company, working on a train. A customer says a parcel never came and wants the money back. The agent opens the case on a laptop and starts clicking: a reason, a receipt, a note. Each click waits for the company's server, on another continent.

Then the train goes into a tunnel. The spinner turns for five seconds, and the app says it couldn't save. Three clicks are gone, and must be done again.

It's easy to blame the network and ask for a retry button. But the app was built so that nothing counts until a faraway server agrees, and a network that comes and goes is normal for a laptop or a phone.

In Many leaders, each region got its own leader and had to deal with conflicts. In this lesson, every laptop and phone becomes a leader, and its copy can run hours behind. We'll let a server decide the order, then merge two people's typing without one. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an agent on a train, losing three clicks to a tunnel. With a copy on the laptop, every click shows in one frame, and the tunnel becomes a delay. Then something has to decide the order: the server, for anything with a rule, or the data type itself, for text that everyone types into.

On your phone, open a notes app that syncs, switch on flight mode, edit a note, and switch flight mode off. Watch whether your edit waits, merges, or asks you to choose.

Next, we'll remove the leader altogether, and find out how a store can know a read is up to date when any copy may take a write.

compare.title: The same two edits to "pay 40": OT and a CRDT

a.label: Operational transformation
a.title: Operational transformation
a.html:
a sends: insert '$' at 4
b sends: insert '!' at 6

at a: b's index 6 is behind a's insert at 4 -> transform to 7
      "pay $40" + insert '!' at 7 = "pay $40!"
at b: a's index 4 is before 6 -> unchanged
      "pay 40!" + insert '$' at 4 = "pay $40!"

per-character metadata: none
needs: an agreed order of edits, usually a server

b.label: CRDT (RGA)
b.title: CRDT (RGA)
b.html:
a sends: insert '$' named 7a after 4a
b sends: insert '!' named 7b after 6a

at a: find 6a, put '!' after it          = "pay $40!"
at b: find 4a, put '$' after it          = "pay $40!"

per-character metadata: an id for every character
                        ever typed, tombstones included
needs: only that 4a and 6a arrive first; no server

compare.note: Both give pay $40!. OT keeps the document cheap and moves the work to merge time: every pair of edits made at the same time is transformed, which is fast for live typing through a server and slow for branches that were edited apart for days. A CRDT pays up front, with an id for every character and tombstones it keeps, and in return any site can merge any edits in any order. Eg-walker's idea is to store edits the way OT does, and build CRDT data only for the stretch edited at the same time, while merging.

worked.title: Choosing a sync design for a dispute console

steps.say: List what the console shows and changes, who changes it, and what should happen when two agents change the same thing.
steps.code:
data                  edited by          two concurrent edits should...
status, assignee      agents             follow the server's rules (no edits after close)
refund decision       senior agents      never merge: one decision, checked by the server
case notes            several agents     both survive, character by character
reason codes          nobody (reference) never conflict: read-only on the device

steps.say: Status, assignee and refunds go through server reconciliation. The client runs mutations optimistically; your server runs the same mutation with the real rules, in one order, and may reject it.
steps.code: // the server half, in your own backend: runs in a transaction, in arrival order fun addNote(tx: Tx, disputeId: String, text: String) { val dispute = tx.load(disputeId) check(dispute.status != Status.CLOSED) { "dispute $disputeId is closed" } // rejected: the client rolls back tx.insertNote(disputeId, text) }

steps.say: Case notes are free text that several people type into at once, sometimes offline. A text CRDT (Automerge or Yjs) merges them on every device, and the server stores the merged document like any other file, without understanding it.
steps.code:
notes: one CRDT document per dispute
  device: apply local keystrokes, send changes, merge incoming ones
  server: relay and store changes; no rules about text

steps.say: Reference data, such as the list of reason codes, only ever flows down. A read-only subset (Electric's shapes, PowerSync's synced tables) keeps it on the device with no way to write it.
steps.code: reason_codes, merchant names: synced down, read-only on the device

steps.say: Decide what never reaches the device. The local copy holds only the disputes this agent may see. Card numbers (PANs, the long number printed on a card) stay on the server, and the console shows the last four digits.
steps.code:
synced to agent 77's laptop:   disputes assigned to team chargebacks, last 30 days
never synced:                  PANs, other teams' disputes, audit log

lab.title: Merge concurrent text edits with OT and with a CRDT
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All 10 fail with NotImplementedError.

In Transform.kt, write transform. Three tests pass, including a jqwik property, a test that makes many random edits at the same time on two sites, runs them through the given transformBoth grid, and checks that both sites end with the same text.
Read RgaText.kt. insert, delete, receive (which holds an edit until the character it names has arrived) and metadataBytes are given.

Write integrate: find the character the insert names, skip nodes with bigger ids, and insert. Then integrateDelete, which only sets the tombstone flag. The rest pass, including a property that three sites agree whatever order edits arrive in, and the extra-data test: 1,000 typed, 500 deleted, 12 bytes per visible character.
Experiment: make integrateDelete remove the node instead of marking it. Run the tests, read which ones fail and why, and put it back.
hints: transform: shift when against.index < op.index, or when the indexes are equal and against.site < op.site. Return op.copy(index = op.index + 1).
In integrate, return at once if has(op.id): the same edit can arrive twice.
The starting point is nodes.indexOfFirst { it.id == op.after } + 1, or 0 when op.after is null.
Then while (at < nodes.size && nodes[at].id > op.id) at++, and nodes.add(at, Node(op.id, op.char)). CharId is Comparable, so > works.
integrateDelete is one line: nodes.first { it.id == op.id }.deleted = true.

drill.title: Transform and integrate from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write (a) transform(op, against) for two inserts made at the same time, with a tie rule, and (b) the RGA rule for where an insert from another site goes. Then say in one line each what OT and the CRDT must keep around, and what each needs from the network.

answer.html: // (a) OT: against was applied first; move op past it if it landed before op's index fun transform(op: Insert, against: Insert): Insert = if (against.index < op.index || (against.index == op.index && against.site < op.site)) op.copy(index = op.index + 1) else op // (b) RGA: start after the named predecessor, skip bigger ids, insert there fun integrate(op: Op.Ins) { if (has(op.id)) return var at = if (op.after == null) 0 else nodes.indexOfFirst { it.id == op.after } + 1 while (at < nodes.size && nodes[at].id > op.id) at++ nodes.add(at, Node(op.id, op.char)) } // OT keeps: no per-character data; needs: one agreed order of edits (a server) // CRDT keeps: an id per character ever typed, tombstones too; needs: predecessor delivered first

recap: A sync engine keeps a copy on the device, so reads and writes finish within a frame, and offline is only copying that runs late. It's multi-leader replication with a leader on each device.
Local-first (Ink & Switch, 2019) asks for more than working offline: the app and your data keep working without the company's servers, which needs an open sync protocol.

Server reconciliation (Linear, Replicache and Zero, PowerSync) runs each mutation optimistically on the client, then for real on the server, in one order. The client rebases its waiting mutations on the server's state and rolls back rejected ones. ElectricSQL syncs reads only, from Postgres logical replication.

OT sends edits by position and transforms each against the ones made at the same time (insert '!' at 6 becomes 7 after an insert at 4). It needs an agreed order, usually a server, and is slow to merge branches edited apart for days.

A text CRDT names every character and inserts after a named character, so edits merge in any order with no server, at the cost of ids and tombstones kept forever. Automerge 3 cut a Moby Dick paste from 700 MB to 1.3 MB; Eg-walker merges in 24 ms what took OT an hour.
The limit: CRDTs promise that copies agree, not that the result is what anyone meant or that a business rule holds. Keep anything with a rule on the server's side of the line.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why Linear-style sync engines don't need CRDTs for most of their data, while two people typing in the same text usually do. Explain.
explain.answer: In a Linear-style engine, the server is a single leader. Every client applies its own changes optimistically so the screen updates at once, but the server runs each change again, one at a time in the order they arrive, with the real rules, and gives every accepted change an increasing sync id. Clients rebuild their state from that log and run again whatever is still waiting, and a rejected change is rolled back. Because one place orders everything, there's never a pair of versions to merge, only a guess to replace. That works well for fields like status or assignee, where one value should win and rules must be checked. Text is different. When two people type into the same paragraph at once, both expect every character to survive, and choosing one version of the paragraph throws the other person's typing away. So text needs a finer merge. Operational transformation adjusts each edit's position against the ones made at the same time, usually through a server. A CRDT gives every character an id and inserts relative to ids, so edits merge in any order, offline, even with no server, at the cost of keeping ids and tombstones.

deeper.html:
Typing that gets shuffled together. RGA's "bigger id first" rule keeps a run of characters typed by one person together. Other text CRDTs can interleave typing done at the same spot: two people typing "abc" and "xyz" at once could end up with "axbycz". Later algorithms such as Fugue were designed to rule that out, and Eg-walker shares that property. Yjs uses its own algorithm, YATA, and is the library behind many editors that run in a web browser.

The counters. The counters in this lesson's CRDT are Lamport clocks: a site's next counter is one more than the highest it has seen. They give every character one order that respects "typed after", without any shared clock. The Faults, time and truth track's lesson on logical clocks builds them properly, together with the version vectors that lesson 8 of this track uses to spot writes made at the same time.

Further reading. The Eg-walker paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14252) is readable and has the numbers: memory in use, load time and merge time against OT and against the best CRDTs, on records of real editing. The Ink & Switch essay (https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/) is longer but worth an evening. It grades Google Docs, Dropbox, Git, Firebase and CouchDB against the seven ideals, and its findings section is honest about what didn't work in their prototypes. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6, places sync engines inside multi-leader replication and covers the OT and CRDT families.
